Skater
SKAY-ter
noun (Gen X slang)
From skate (Dutch schaats) + -er; as the name of a youth subculture it means a skateboarder. Skateboarding began among California surfers in the late 1950s and 1960s; its Gen X form was born in the Santa Monica and Venice "Dogtown" of the mid-1970s, where the Zephyr team (the Z-Boys) rode drained backyard swimming pools during the 1976–77 drought. Thrasher magazine (San Francisco, 1981) gave the scene its motto, "Skate and Destroy," and Powell Peralta’s Bones Brigade (Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, Rodney Mullen) and its videos (from 1984) gave it heroes. Skater style: Vans, baggy shorts, a board under the arm, a punk tape in the Walkman.

Biblical Definition

A skater in Gen X speech was more than a boy with a skateboard; he was a member of a tribe, with its own magazines, music, shoes, and contempt for "No Skateboarding" signs. The scene had a defiant edge ("Skate and Destroy"), a love of empty lots and drained pools, and a deep loyalty among friends. The Christian observation is that most of what made a skater is good. Skating is hard; it is learned only by falling, hundreds of times, and getting back up. Scripture honors that pattern: "a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16), and the believer who stumbles "shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand" (Psa 37:24). The Preacher would approve the skater’s focus: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). Where the culture needs examining is its attitude toward authority and property. The "Skateboarding is not a crime" bumper sticker was clever, but grinding a church handrail after the sign says no is not innocence. "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers" (Rom 13:1). And the skill, wonderful as it is, has a ceiling: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). A father can stand at the skate park and cheer every fall-and-rise, then tell his son: you already know how to get up after a fall; learn to do it before God, and learn to respect the sign.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X name (mid-1970s Dogtown, Thrasher 1981) for a skateboarder and his tribe; Scripture honors the fall-and-rise of the skater (Pro 24:16) and asks him to respect the sign as well (Rom 13:1).

SKATER, n. (Gen X slang, mid-1970s–1990s, Southern California) A skateboarder, especially one who belongs to the skateboarding subculture with its music, dress, and attitude. "The skaters took over the bank parking lot every Sunday."

Also skate rat, sk8r; Dogtown, Z-Boys, Bones Brigade; tricks: ollie, kickflip, grind, rail slide.

Badges: Thrasher magazine (from 1981, "Skate and Destroy"), Vans sneakers, punk and hip-hop soundtracks, "Skateboarding is not a crime."

Webster 1828: SKATE, n. A sort or shoe furnished with a smooth iron for sliding on ice.

Decode for parents: the skater has learned perseverance by falling; teach him to apply it to the soul and to honor the property line.

Key Scripture

Pro 24:16 — "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief."

Psa 37:24 — "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand."

Ecc 9:10 — "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

1Ti 4:8 — "For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come."

Modern Corruption

Skater culture prizes the good discipline of falling and rising but can wear contempt for authority and property as a badge; Scripture keeps the perseverance and corrects the contempt.

expand to see more

"Skate and Destroy." The scene’s motto was half joke, half creed. Trespassing in empty pools, grinding the bank’s ledges, and dodging security guards became part of the identity, and the outlaw thrill was much of the fun. But a property owner’s sign and a policeman’s word are not enemies of freedom; the powers that be are ordained of God (Rom 13:1). A Christian skater can ride with everything he has and still go where he is welcome.

The best thing a skater knows. No one lands a trick without falling on it a hundred times. That is the most biblical lesson in the whole subculture: the just man falls seven times and rises up again (Pro 24:16), and the LORD upholds the one who falls (Psa 37:24). Bodily skill profits a little (1Ti 4:8); the same grit turned toward repentance, prayer, and obedience profits for this life and the next. A father who has watched his son bleed for a kickflip already knows the boy can endure; he only needs to show him the race worth enduring for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Dutch schaats → English skate → 1960s sidewalk surfing → mid-1970s Dogtown Z-Boys → Thrasher (1981) and the Bones Brigade → Gen X skater tribe; Scripture: falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16).

Dutch schaats — skate; English skate (17th c.), ice skate

Late 1950s–1960s California: skateboarding as "sidewalk surfing"

Mid-1970s Santa Monica and Venice: Dogtown, the Zephyr team, pool riding in the 1976–77 drought

1981 Thrasher; 1984 onward Bones Brigade videos; skater names the tribe

Biblical perseverance: the just man riseth up again (Pro 24:16); the LORD upholdeth (Psa 37:24)

Usage

""Skaters aren’t allowed at the mall anymore." — c. 1988."

"A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16) — every skater already knows the first half."

"Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers (Rom 13:1), even the one who posted the sign."
